aspects.says: new String creates a heap object even when the literal is pooled, and Integer.valueOf caches only -128 to 127.
aspects.reason: incidental detail, not practised; comparing with equals, which the Common Data Structures page practises, makes these caches irrelevant

aspects.says: try-with-resources closes a resource even when the body throws.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
aspects.reason: incidental here: the page lists it as one leak pattern, and closing is a language construct with nothing memory-specific to grade

aspects.says: HotSpot never allocates a whole object on the stack; escape analysis can instead remove a non-escaping allocation by scalar replacement.
A data structure that keeps a reference to a removed element keeps it reachable, so a stack's pop must null out the freed slot.
basis: section:Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

aspects.says: Java passes the value of a reference, so a method can change the caller's object but reassigning its parameter never changes the caller's variable.
Soft references are cleared only under memory pressure, weak references by the first collection that finds them weakly reachable, and a phantom reference's get() is always null.
Static collections and listeners that are never removed keep objects reachable; bounded caches, WeakHashMap and deregistration fix them.
aspects.reason: whether memory is freed shows only after a garbage collection, whose timing no test can control; the bounded LRU cache is practised on the Common Data Structures page

aspects.says: StackOverflowError comes from call depth in one thread and OutOfMemoryError from an exhausted shared heap.
aspects.reason: deep-chain practises the StackOverflowError half; exhausting the heap in a test depends on the runner's heap size and is not deterministic

aspects.says: The stack is per thread and holds frames with primitives and references; the heap is shared and holds every object, and the String pool lives in it.
aspects.reason: where a value lives is not observable from Java code, so a reader's program cannot be graded on it; the practices grade its consequences (shared objects, frame depth)

aspects.says: Each call pushes a frame on the thread's small stack, so recursion as deep as the data throws StackOverflowError, and converting it to a loop avoids that.
Virtual threads keep small, growable stacks on the heap, but -Xss still caps how deep they can go.
